segments.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks.
A missing twelve-year-old girl's mummified remains were discovered nearly two months later in an abandoned Florida hog shed.
That's where this story ends.
Today we're going back to the beginning — to understand how it got there.
Ted Bundy is believed to have murdered at least 30 young women between 1974 and 1978.
His crimes spanned Washington, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Idaho, and Florida.
That's not a spree.
That's a campaign, carried out over four years, across half a dozen states.
The modus operandi was methodical.
Bundy would approach his victims while wearing an arm sling or cast, using a false pretext — asking someone to help him carry books, for example.
Once he had them close to his Volkswagen Beetle, he'd bludgeon them unconscious, typically with a crowbar, then drive them to a pre-selected secluded location.
What the evidence actually shows is a man who understood how to weaponize trust.
He looked approachable.
He asked for help.
And by the time a victim understood what was happening, it was too late.
That pattern held across state lines, across years, and ultimately, it held in Lake City, Florida, in February 1978.
Let's unpack it.
The timeline leading up to Lake City is crucial.
In early 1977, Bundy was in custody in Colorado, facing a murder charge.
He was acting as his own attorney.
That gave him access to the law library at the Pitkin County Courthouse.
On June 7, 1977, he jumped from a second-story window while the guard was on a smoke break.
He vanished into the mountains for six days before being recaptured.
Six months later, he did it again.
On December 30, 1977, he slipped through a gap in the ceiling of his cell at the Garfield County Jail in Glenwood Springs.
He boarded a flight to Chicago, took a train to Michigan, drove to Atlanta, and caught a bus to Tallahassee.
He made it to Tallahassee before anyone knew he was gone.
He was added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on February 10, 1978, over a month after his escape.
That brings us to February 9, 1978.
Kimberly Diane Leach was twelve years old.
She was in the seventh grade.
That morning, she vanished from her junior high school in Lake City.
The case file shows that multiple eyewitnesses came forward.
They reported seeing a white van circling the school.
More importantly, they saw an adult man leading a young girl to that van and driving off.
Six days after Kimberly disappeared, a police officer in Pensacola spotted a suspicious car at 1:30 in the morning.
He ran the plates.
The orange Volkswagen was stolen.
After a brief scuffle, the driver was arrested.
He refused to give his real name, handing over a stolen driver's license and claiming he was an FSU student named Kenneth.
It took two days in custody before he finally revealed his true identity to authorities.
Investigators quickly connected him to the disappearance in Lake City.
They found a stolen white van tied to him.
Fiber analysis showed a two-way transfer.
Analysts found fibers matching Kimberly's clothing inside the van.
Fibers from his clothing were later found on her body.
The physical evidence was locking into place.
To understand how a man ends up driving a stolen car through Pensacola with a fake ID, we have to look at where the timeline actually starts.
The record points to early 1974.
That winter, young women began disappearing at an alarming rate across the state of Washington.
The first was a twenty-one-year-old undergraduate at the University of Washington named Lynda Ann Healy.
On February 1, she vanished from her basement room in Seattle.
The case file shows this was the only disappearance in the early cluster that left behind physical evidence.
Investigators found a blood-stained mattress and a nightgown left behind in her room.
Just over a month later, the pattern repeated further south.
On March 12, nineteen-year-old Donna Gail Manson disappeared in Olympia.
She was a student at The Evergreen State College who vanished while going to attend a campus jazz concert.
Building a timeline for her last known whereabouts was incredibly difficult for law enforcement.
She was not reported missing for six days.
Her peers knew she frequently hitchhiked to nearby towns, so they initially assumed she had just traveled without sharing her plans.
Detectives also knew she was depressed, meaning they could not completely rule out the slim possibility that she had left to end her own life.
The disappearances kept happening.
On April 17, eighteen-year-old Susan Elaine Rancourt vanished in Ellensburg.
She disappeared off the Central Washington State College campus right after leaving a dorm advisors meeting.
With no bodies found and very few clues to go on, law enforcement officials were baffled.
Given the limits of forensic technology in the 1970s, these cases were incredibly complex to piece together.
But detectives began to notice undeniable connections between the missing women.
The victims shared very specific physical characteristics.
They were all young, slender Caucasian women who parted their long hair in the middle.
Healy had waist-length chestnut hair, and Manson had long dark brown hair, though Rancourt stood out slightly with blonde hair.
They all came from stable backgrounds and were considered gifted or of above-average intelligence.
During the times they vanished, all of them were reportedly wearing slacks.
They were taken in the hours of darkness, always within a week of a midterm or final exam at a local college.
Strangely enough, investigators also noted that construction work was being done on each girl's respective campus when she disappeared.
The radius of the disappearances was about to expand.
On May 6, twenty-year-old Oregon State University student Roberta Kathleen Parks vanished in Corvallis.
She left her dormitory that evening to meet friends at a local coffee shop and never arrived.
Captain Herb Swindler was convinced her disappearance was linked to the others.
She had hip-length hair parted in the middle, though hers was ash blonde.
But other law enforcement officials doubted the connection, feeling Corvallis was simply too far away from the Washington colleges.
Police also knew Parks had a history of mood swings and was feeling homesick.
She had recently broken up with her boyfriend.
Just two days before she went missing, she got into a verbal altercation with her father, who suffered a near-fatal heart attack that exact same day.
Because of her mental state, investigators couldn't rule out the possibility that she had taken her own life.
They briefly considered the nearby Willamette River as a place of interest.
The river was dragged, but searchers found absolutely nothing.
Less than a month later, the timeline shifts back up to Washington state.
On June 1, twenty-two-year-old Brenda Carol Ball disappeared in Burien.
She was last seen leaving a place called the Flame Tavern.
Like some of the earlier cases, Ball wasn't reported missing right away.
She was known to have an adventurous spirit.
People in her life thought she might have just taken off on a whim, delaying the start of any official search.
Ten days later, the pattern struck the University of Washington again.
Eighteen-year-old Georgann Hawkins vanished in Seattle on the night of June 11.
She disappeared from an alley right behind her Kappa Alpha Theta sorority house.
Hawkins was a former Daffodil Princess and a straight-A student who dreamed of becoming a broadcast journalist.
She was petite, standing just five feet two inches tall, with long brown hair.
She had a steady boyfriend at a nearby fraternity and rarely walked around the campus alone at night.
The case file shows she had clear, concrete plans for her immediate future.
She had just secured a summer job back in her hometown of Tacoma to help pay for her second year of studies.
She intended to head home just two days after she disappeared, and her job was set to start on June 17.
The missing persons reports were piling up, and the summer was just beginning.
The missing persons reports were piling up, but the Washington disappearances ultimately culminated on a single Sunday.
The date was July 14, 1974.
The location was Lake Sammamish State Park.
Janice Ann Ott was a twenty-three-year-old probation case worker.
She was married, and she was spending the day lying on the beach.
Witnesses noticed a handsome man approach her.
He was wearing tennis shorts, a white shirt, and tennis shoes, and he had his arm in a sling.
The man asked Janice for help.
He told her he needed to load his sailboat onto his car, which was parked at his parents' house in Issaquah.
Janice hesitated because she had her bicycle with her and didn't want it stolen, but the man assured her the bike would fit in his trunk.
People nearby overheard the exchange.
Janice agreed to help and walked away with him.
She was wearing cutoff jeans and a white shirt tied over a black bikini.
As they left, one witness heard them exchange names, with the man introducing himself as Ted.
Four hours later, the exact same park became a crime scene again.
Denise Marie Naslund was a nineteen-year-old computer programming student.
She was at Lake Sammamish having a picnic with her boyfriend, another couple, and her dog.
Around 4:30 that afternoon, Denise left her group to use the restroom.
She took her dog with her.
She was wearing cutoff shorts and a blue halter top, leaving her sandals behind on the beach.
Sometime later, her dog found its way back to her friends alone.
Nobody actually saw Denise leave the park with a man in a sling.
But people who knew her told investigators she had a tender-hearted, friendly personality.
They said she would have gladly helped an injured stranger without a second thought.
That generated an absolute media frenzy.
Suddenly, several other women between the ages of fifteen and twenty-six came forward with their own stories.
They told police they had been approached at the park by a man named Ted who spoke with a slight British accent.
He asked for help with a sailboat.
One witness actually walked with him to the parking lot.
She told investigators he led her to a metallic brown Volkswagen Bug.
When she pointed out there was no sailboat on the car, he claimed it was just up the hill at his folks' house.
That witness backed out, telling him she had to wait for her husband.
The aftermath of Lake Sammamish changed the entire investigation.
That massive media frenzy finally gave detectives a concrete profile to work with.
They were no longer looking for a ghost.
They were actively hunting this 'Ted', who used an arm sling to lure women with a fake sailboat.
The case file shows just how brazen this campaign was.
A friend of earlier victim Georgann Hawkins, a woman named Phyllis Armstrong, later shared a terrifying detail.
She said the man had actually approached her, asking for help with his car, just a few days before Hawkins vanished.
He was testing his methods in plain sight.
But just as the public in Washington went on high alert for a man named Ted driving a brown Volkswagen, the geography of the disappearances shifted.
In the summer of 1974, he moved to Salt Lake City.
He enrolled as a law student at the University of Utah.
The change in scenery did not slow down the violence.
It actually accelerated it.
Over a span of just five weeks, four more young women were murdered in Utah.
Sixteen-year-old Nancy Wilcox vanished in Holladay.
Seventeen-year-old Melissa Smith disappeared in Midvale.
Laura Ann Aime, also seventeen, was taken in Lehi.
And seventeen-year-old Debra Jean Kent vanished in Bountiful.
What the evidence actually shows is that the tactics were evolving.
He was not just relying on the injured arm routine anymore.
On November 8, 1974, an eighteen-year-old named Carol DaRonch was at a shopping mall in Murray, Utah.
A man approached her, but this time, he was posing as a police officer.
He told DaRonch someone had attempted to break into her vehicle.
He insisted she needed to come with him to the Murray Police Department to sign an official complaint.
She trusted his authority, and they drove off in his Volkswagen Beetle.
They never made it to a police station.
He eventually pulled the car over and tried to force handcuffs onto her wrists.
He managed to get one cuff secured and threatened her with a gun.
DaRonch fought for her life.
She jumped out of the Volkswagen and flagged down a passing vehicle.
An elderly couple picked her up and drove her straight to the authorities.
For the first time, a victim had escaped, and she was able to give police a direct, detailed description of her attacker.
Carol DaRonch escaping was a massive break in the investigation.
She gave police a direct, detailed description of the man and his Volkswagen Beetle.
What makes that timeline so chilling is what happened next.
The record shows that was just hours after DaRonch got away.
We already know about the string of murders that hit Utah in the late summer and fall of 1974.
We know he was behind the disappearances of Nancy Wilcox, Melissa Smith, Laura Ann Aime, and Debra Jean Kent.
He was balancing his legal studies with a relentless, five-week campaign of violence.
By 1975, that campaign crossed state lines again.
The geography expanded into Colorado and Idaho.
On January 12, a twenty-three-year-old nurse named Caryn Campbell was vacationing with her fiancé in Snowmass Village, Colorado.

Law enforcement agencies across multiple states were dealing with missing women, but they didn't have a name to connect them.
That finally changed in the early hours of August 16, 1975.
Utah Highway Patrol Sergeant Bob Hayward was finishing his shift in Granger.

The driver immediately took off.
Sergeant Hayward chased the vehicle down and pulled it over.

The driver was arrested for evading an officer.
The law student was finally in custody.
We already know about the eighteen-year-old who fought for her life in a Volkswagen Beetle.

Remember, she flagged down that elderly couple just hours before Debra Jean Kent disappeared.
She gave investigators a clear description of the driver and his car.
Now, in August of 1975, Utah Highway Patrol had that exact car impounded.
The driver was sitting in a jail cell.
Detectives organized a police lineup and brought DaRonch in to take a look.
The case file notes that he actually made attempts to alter his appearance before standing in that lineup.
It did not work.
DaRonch looked at the men and identified him as the person who attacked her.
On October 2, he was officially charged with aggravated kidnapping and attempted criminal assault.
The man who had been hunting young women across multiple states was finally facing a bench trial.
That trial took place in 1976.
The evidence held up in court.
He was found guilty of aggravated kidnapping and sentenced to serve between one and fifteen years in a Utah state prison.
While he was sitting in that cell, the broader investigation was gaining momentum.
Sheriffs from neighboring counties, including up in Washington, were looking closely at the Utah inmate.
They strongly suspected he was the same man responsible for the string of unsolved murders in the Pacific Northwest.

Investigators executed a search of his impounded Volkswagen Beetle and found hairs inside the vehicle.

Based on that physical evidence, he was officially charged with first-degree murder in Campbell's death.
